Meanwhile a database cache keeps hot rows near the application; it cuts trips to disk and shrinks latency for busy services. Engineers often tune how long each entry stays before expiry, since stale answers can mislead users at any time.

However a cache can also go wrong when writes update the database but leave old copies alive in memory. Teams call this invalidation, and it is famously hard. Strategies include write-through, write-behind, and time-based expiry; each trades speed against freshness. A cache miss forces a read from the source, while a cache hit saves work.

Along with that, most apps lack a tiny pool of fast data. Such hits cut load and boost flow. Still, a shot of logic adds risk. All tasks with hot data gain from a snap of quick hits. Also, a mirror of truth must hold up.

Finally a cache must be sized and tested; otherwise, speed hides bugs, so verify every path before calling it done.
